MSK-SKIN · HISTOPATHOLOGY LAB

PNS & Connective Tissue Histopath Lab

Lecture Companion · Keloid, Schwannoma, and Neurofibroma

Learning objectives

Note: the provided lab deck does not state formal learning objectives, so these are reconstructed strictly from the material it teaches.

  • Recognize the clinical and histologic features that distinguish a keloid from a hypertrophic scar.
  • Recognize the gross, radiologic, and microscopic pattern of schwannoma, including Antoni A, Antoni B, and Verocay bodies.
  • Recognize the clinical and microscopic pattern of neurofibroma and distinguish localized, diffuse, and plexiform types.
  • Connect schwannoma with NF2 and neurofibroma—especially plexiform neurofibroma—with NF1.
  • Use the characteristic histologic clue in each lesion to identify it when labels are removed.

Big Picture

This lab is fundamentally a pattern-recognition exercise. The three lesions can all look “fibrous” or “spindled,” but the key is to attach each lesion to its own architecture:

Keloid → thick, glassy eosinophilic collagen   |   Schwannoma → alternating Antoni A/B with Verocay bodies   |   Neurofibroma → haphazard wavy cells + “shredded carrot” collagen

Then layer on the clinical associations: keloids grow beyond the original wound, bilateral vestibular schwannomas point to NF2, and a plexiform neurofibroma is pathognomonic of NF1.

1. Keloid

MUST KNOW

Clinical identity

  • A keloid is a scar-like lesion that extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound.
  • This is the course's key distinction from a hypertrophic scar, which stays within the original wound.
  • It is more common in patients with darker skin pigmentation, though it can occur in anyone.
  • The earlobe is identified as the most common site in the lecture.
  • Biopsy is usually not required for diagnosis.
HIGH YIELD

Histology: “keloidal” collagen

The lesion is large, nodular, and dermal based. Its defining microscopic feature is “keloidal” collagen: thickened, homogeneous, hyalinized/glassy, deeply eosinophilic bands of collagen.

Image recognition: If the labels are removed, look for broad, intensely pink, glassy collagen bundles that appear unusually thick and relatively acellular compared with ordinary scar tissue.
CLINICAL CONNECTION

Why it behaves differently

For exam purposes, the behavior matters as much as the appearance: the process does not respect the original wound edge, so the scar grows outward into surrounding skin.

TREATMENT

Course management

Direct steroid injection is often first line. Surgical excision may be used, commonly with concurrent steroid injections or radiotherapy to reduce recurrence.

EXAM TRAP

Prognosis

Persistence and recurrence are common, but the lecture explicitly states no risk of malignancy.

Retrieval checkpoint: A scar extends beyond the original wound and recurs after treatment. What histologic feature should you expect?
Answer: thick, homogeneous, hyalinized, deeply eosinophilic “keloidal” collagen.

2. Schwannoma

MUST KNOW

Core concept

A schwannoma is a benign nerve sheath tumor of Schwann cells, the myelinating cells of the PNS. Most are sporadic, but the lecture links a minority to inherited syndromes.

  • NF2: bilateral vestibular schwannomas (“acoustic neuromas”) and multiple schwannomas.
  • Schwannomatosis: another syndrome associated with multiple schwannomas.
  • Removal is described as curative.
  • Radiology: a well-circumscribed mass with heterogeneous enhancement, corresponding to variable cellularity, arising from a nerve.
HIGH YIELD

Histologic architecture

  • Spindled cells with tapered ends; cells may appear wavy.
  • Antoni A: hypercellular areas with compact spindle cells ± Verocay bodies.
  • Antoni B: hypocellular areas made of loose-textured cell processes.
  • Hyalinized, thick-walled vessels may be present.
  • Mucin deposition, “ancient change” (degenerative nuclear atypia), and lymphoid aggregates in the capsule may occur.
Schwannoma = organized alternation: dense Antoni A ↔ loose Antoni B
MUST KNOW

Verocay body

Within Antoni A regions, nuclei form palisades on either side of an acellular/anuclear zone. That organized nuclear alignment is the visual clue.

Look for: parallel rows of elongated nuclei → central pale acellular zone → another nuclear palisade.
FIRST AID CONNECTION

Board-level pattern

Lecture concept: schwannoma is a benign Schwann-cell tumor; NF2 is linked to bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

What First Aid adds: schwannomas classically arise at the cerebellopontine angle or along peripheral nerves; vestibular schwannomas can present with hearing loss, tinnitus, and unsteady gait. First Aid also emphasizes S-100 positivity and the same biphasic hypercellular/hypocellular pattern.

Why it matters: a pathology image plus unilateral auditory symptoms points toward vestibular schwannoma; bilateral vestibular tumors strongly redirect the question toward NF2.

Retrieval checkpoint: A nerve sheath tumor alternates between tightly packed spindle-cell areas and loose hypocellular areas. Name the two patterns.
Answer: Antoni A (hypercellular) and Antoni B (hypocellular).
Retrieval checkpoint: What microscopic structure is made of nuclear palisades separated by an anuclear zone?
Answer: Verocay body.

3. Neurofibroma

MUST KNOW

Core concept

A neurofibroma is a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor composed of Schwann cells, fibroblasts, and perineurial cells. It may retain residual nerve axons and may contain abundant extracellular matrix.

  • The lecture identifies it as the most common peripheral nerve sheath tumor.
  • About 90% are sporadic; about 10% are associated with syndromes such as NF1.
  • It is benign and can recur locally.
  • Malignant transformation can rarely occur.
HIGH YIELD

Histology

  • Loosely arranged spindle cells in a haphazard pattern.
  • Schwann-cell nuclei are hyperchromatic, small, wavy, buckled, or “comma shaped.”
  • Fibroblasts and other cell types are admixed.
  • Interspersed collagen fibers create the classic “shredded carrot” appearance.
  • Stromal mucin may be present.
Neurofibroma = mixed-cell, loose, haphazard architecture rather than the organized Antoni A/B pattern of schwannoma.
MUST KNOW

Three types of neurofibroma

TypeCourse descriptionBest distinguishing clue
LocalizedSolitary, superficial, slow-growing lesion; usually in patients without NF1.Single superficial lesion
DiffusePlaque-like thickening; may be more cellular; pseudo-Meissnerian bodies can be present.Plaque-like growth
PlexiformMultinodular, serpentine growth; grossly a “bag of worms.”Pathognomonic of NF1; higher malignant-transformation rate
FIRST AID CONNECTION

NF1 vs NF2

Lecture concept: plexiform neurofibroma is pathognomonic of NF1, while bilateral vestibular schwannomas are linked to NF2.

What First Aid adds: NF1 is associated with neurofibromas plus café-au-lait spots, Lisch nodules, optic gliomas, pheochromocytomas, and other features; NF2 is associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas, and juvenile cataracts.

Why it matters: the tumor type can identify the syndrome before the question gives the gene.

Retrieval checkpoint: Which neurofibroma subtype is pathognomonic of NF1?
Answer: plexiform neurofibroma.
Retrieval checkpoint: What gross descriptor should immediately make you think of plexiform neurofibroma?
Answer: “bag of worms.”

MSK CONNECTION

Master these before moving on

  1. Keloid boundary rule: keloid extends beyond the original wound; hypertrophic scar does not. This is the fastest clinical discriminator.
  2. Schwannoma architecture: Antoni A = dense, Antoni B = loose; Verocay bodies live in the organized hypercellular component.
  3. Neurofibroma texture: loose wavy spindle cells + admixed cell types + shredded-carrot collagen.
  4. NF split: NF1 → plexiform neurofibroma; NF2 → bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

The most useful First Aid connections

  • Vestibular schwannoma: hearing loss, tinnitus, unsteady gait.
  • Schwannoma: S-100 positive; hypercellular and hypocellular regions.
  • NF2: bilateral vestibular schwannomas + meningiomas/ependymomas/juvenile cataracts.
  • NF1: cutaneous neurofibromas plus classic neurocutaneous findings.
